chunks: Ibn Abi Umayr narrated from Jamil, from Bakir, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them) who said:

Verily Adam (peace be upon him) said: 'O Lord, You allowed Shaytan to prevail over me and made him flow in me like blood, so grant me something.' He said: 'O Adam, I have granted you that whoever among your progeny intends an evil deed, it will not be recorded against him; if he does it, one evil deed is recorded against him. And whoever among them intends a good deed, if he does not do it, one good deed is recorded for him; and if he does it, ten good deeds are recorded for him.' He said: 'O Lord, give me more.' He said: 'I have granted you that whoever among them commits an evil deed and then seeks forgiveness, I shall forgive him.' He said: 'O Lord, give me more.' He said: 'I have granted them repentance' (or he said: 'I have extended their repentance until the soul reaches here [the throat]'). He said: 'O Lord, that is sufficient for me.'

key_terms.النفس: The soul (specifically referring to the soul reaching the throat at death)

ai.seo_question: What are the stages of divine forgiveness and recording of deeds according to the dialogue between Adam and God?
ai.summary: This hadith, transmitted through the chain of al-Ahwazi’s *Kitab al-Zuhd*, elucidates the theological concept of *al-Ham* (inner intention) as the precursor to *al-'Amal* (action), a key distinction in Shia jurisprudence for determining when a sin is recorded. It emphasizes the divine generosity in multiplying good deeds tenfold while accepting sincere repentance (*tawbah*) as a continuous state until the soul reaches the throat (*hulqum*), a specific sign of imminent death in Shia tradition. The dialogue underscores that forgiveness is not merely a post-facto remedy but an inherent attribute of God’s mercy extended to Adam’s progeny.
